L01.title: Compiler-error practice
L01.intro: Original practice for the Chapter 1 skills. Keep the already-posted Lab Exercise 5 and quiz submission instructions; this activity adds no retrospective submission.
steps: Save the baseline as Hello.java, compile it, and run it. Record the filename, public class name, main header, and exact output.
Predict the effect of deleting the print statement’s semicolon. Make only that change, compile, record the first error, and restore the baseline.
Repeat with a missing closing quotation mark, then with println changed to Println. Restore the baseline between experiments.
Change only the greeting text. Explain the difference between code that cannot compile and code that runs but prints an unintended message.
For each experiment, record the edit, your prediction, whether compilation succeeded, the observed message/output, and the repair.
checks: The restored baseline compiles and prints Hello, Java! on one line.
Each experiment changes only one feature, so your explanation identifies a cause.
L01.evidence: Keep your experiment table and restored Hello.java with your Chapter 1 notes. Use the original Classroom assignment for any required Lab 5 submission.

L02.title: Addition and concatenation practice
L02.intro: Original course practice for predicting Java output. Write all six predictions before running the program.
steps: For each print statement, predict the exact output and label each operation as arithmetic or String concatenation.
Run the program. Beside every mismatch, write the first operation you evaluated incorrectly.
Explain why the parentheses in the second statement change the result and why the casts in the last two statements are different.
Change a to 9 and b to 4. Predict all six outputs again before running.
checks: With a = 7 and b = 2, the first two lines are Total: 72 and Total: 9.
With a = 9 and b = 4, casting before division gives 2.25; casting the integer quotient afterward gives 2.0.
L02.evidence: A six-row prediction/observation table, two causal explanations, and your fresh predictions for the second input pair.

L03.title: Circle calculation practice
L03.intro: Original course practice using a constant, numeric input, assignment, and double arithmetic. Assume the entered radius is nonnegative.
steps: Complete the two calculations. Use multiplication for the square; Java’s ^ operator does not mean exponentiation.
Predict area and circumference for radii 1 and 3, using the supplied PI constant. Then run both cases.
Test radius 0 and one fractional radius. Explain why radius and the results use double.
Record each variable’s type and the unit of each result: square units for area and units for circumference.
checks: Radius 0: both results are 0.0. Compare decimal results within 0.00001 to allow for floating-point representation.
L03.evidence: Your completed source, predicted/actual values for two inputs, and a brief explanation of constants and numeric types. Follow the dated lesson for the required submission.

L04.title: Room-paint calculation practice
L04.intro: Original course practice with explicit assumptions: a rectangular room, four walls, one coat, no ceiling, and no deductions for doors or windows. All dimensions are positive feet. Coverage is 350 square feet per gallon; report fractional gallons without rounding up.
steps: Sketch the four walls. Two have area length times height; two have area width times height. Write one expression for their combined area.
Complete wallArea and gallons in the starter, keeping the units visible in your notes.
Predict both outputs for a 10-by-12-by-8 room and a 20-by-15-by-10 room before running the program.
Explain how using integer division could lose the fractional amount. State which assumptions would need to change to account for openings or an additional coat.
checks: Length 10, width 12, height 8: wall area 352.0 square feet; approximately 1.005714 gallons.
Length 20, width 15, height 10: wall area 700.0 square feet; 2.0 gallons. Compare decimal results within 0.00001.
L04.evidence: For the September 11 homework, save the completed calculation and two predicted/actual output pairs with your ExpressionLab repair. These are the assumptions for this original practice version.
